draft.title: Prime factorisation with index notation
card: A prime number has exactly two factors, 1 and itself. Examples are 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11.
A factor tree splits a number into factor pairs again and again until every branch ends in a prime. For 72: 72 = 8 × 9, 8 = 2 × 4, 4 = 2 × 2, 9 = 3 × 3.
Multiply the primes at the ends: 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3.
Index form counts repeated primes with a small power. Three 2s make 2³ and two 3s make 3², so 72 = 2³ × 3².
draft.remember: Split into primes, then write repeated primes with an index.

a.q: Which is 40 written as a product of primes in index form?
a.why: 40 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 5, which is 2³ × 5. The option 2² × 10 is wrong because 10 is not a prime, and 2⁴ × 5 equals 80.
a.clue: Keep splitting until every number is prime.

b.q: Dev writes 90 as 2 × 3² × 5. Sam says it is wrong. What should Sam check?
opts: Multiply it out: 2 × 9 × 5 = 90, so Dev is right
Whether 90 needs 5² because it ends in 0
b.why: 3² means 3 × 3 = 9, so 2 × 9 × 5 = 90 and Dev is correct. The idea that 3² is 3 × 2 mixes up the index with multiplying.

b.best: Multiply it out: 2 × 9 × 5 = 90, so Dev is right

problems.detail: The stem asks 'What should Sam check?', but the right option is a verdict ('so Dev is right'), not a check. It is also the only option not starting with 'Whether', and the only one with a worked calculation, so it stands out and can be picked without knowing the idea.
The clue 'Work out 3² first, then multiply' tells the student to do exactly what the right option does, which gives the answer away.

final.title: Prime factorisation with index notation
card: A prime number has exactly two factors, 1 and itself. Examples are 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11.
A factor tree splits a number into factor pairs again and again until every branch ends in a prime. For 72: \(72 = 8 \times 9\), \(8 = 2 \times 4\), \(4 = 2 \times 2\), \(9 = 3 \times 3\).
Multiply the primes at the ends: \(72 = 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3\).
Index form counts repeated primes with a small power. Three 2s make \(2^{3}\) and two 3s make \(3^{2}\), so \(72 = 2^{3} \times 3^{2}\).
final.remember: Split into primes, then write repeated primes with an index.

a.q: Which is 40 written as a product of primes in index form?
a.why: \(40 = 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 5\), which is \(2^{3} \times 5\). The option \(2^{2} \times 10\) is wrong because 10 is not a prime, and \(2^{4} \times 5\) equals 80.
a.clue: Keep splitting until every number is prime.

b.q: Mia writes 180 as a product of primes in index form. Which answer is correct?
b.why: \(180 = 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 5\), which is \(2^{2} \times 3^{2} \times 5\). The option \(2 \times 3^{2} \times 10\) does equal 180, but \(10 = 2 \times 5\) is not a prime, so the tree was not finished. The option \(2^{3} \times 3^{2} \times 5\) equals 360.
b.clue: Check that every number is prime and that the total is 180.
